name: Hana Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the lead operator on the milk bottling line at Brookfield Dairy. I start at five-thirty, run the sanitising cycle, set the filler for the day's bottle size and then spend the shift chasing small stops: a cap jam, a label drifting. I log every stop and I feed the logs into an AI tool each afternoon to see what pattern I missed. My feet hurt, but my head is the busiest it's been in years.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: That's interesting. How did you start using AI at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My granddaughter showed me on my phone two years ago, and I tried it on our stop logs the same week. It found that most of our label jams came after a changeover on Tuesdays. I told the maintenance boss and he fixed a roller. I was hooked after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool that people oversell. At work I tell the others it won't run the line for them but it'll spot patterns faster than any of us. Online I'd be the one saying, try it before you decide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd be a bit disappointed, because I enjoy it. But my life carries on fine either way. I'm 58 with a good pension building and the savings to match.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using it every day for the stop logs and for drafting the changeover checklists. I'd keep training the new starters on the filler. And I'd put a bit more into my pension top-up, since I've got the time to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a little flat, since I like the new stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you use it for now, day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stop analysis, writing up checklists, working out the best order for the day's flavours. I also ask it to explain things in the maintenance manual in plain words.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you worry people are being overly excited about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A few say it's all a fad. I tell them what the Tuesday roller taught me: a small tool can find a big problem.

think: I'd be a little **disappointed**, because I enjoy using it.
My life carries on fine either way, with a good pension building.
do: Keep using AI daily on the **stop logs** and changeover checklists.
Keep training the new starters on the filler.
Put a bit more into my **pension** top-up.
feel: **Calm**, if a little flat, since I like the new tools.
S0.quote: I tell them what the Tuesday roller taught me: a small tool can find a big problem.
fieldNote: She is a daily **user** and values AI as a pattern-spotter for her own work.
Secure, so calm is earned, with a hint of disappointment.
Evangelises to colleagues through concrete stories.

steps.text: Keep feeding the daily stop logs to the AI tool
Keep training new starters on the filler
Top up the pension by a fixed amount each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's already showing up in the planning room. The scheduling and purchasing people would see fewer jobs, and the lab paperwork gets quicker. On my line it changes how we find faults, not whether there's a line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my own role gets better. A lead operator who can read the data and talk to the machine is worth more, not less. I do worry about the quality clerks and the order desk, who are in their forties with kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go further with the tools: ask the firm to let me test a camera-based jam detector, and I'd put my hand up to write the training notes for the others. I'd also teach the desk staff the basics at lunchtime, because I'd rather they were ahead of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. Interested, honestly. It's the people around me I keep thinking about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at the plant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Birgit on the order desk and the two lab clerks. They've got no way to use their skills on the floor yet, and I'd want to help them find a way in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change how you spend your money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my savings steady and not spend on anything big until I see how the firm handles it. No point rushing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's huge and we're not ready. Two years is nothing. I'd tell people to start learning now, not wait to be told, and to push the firm for training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record it scares me more than I let on. The thinking AI in 2028 I can use. But a robot that can run a filler in 2031 is what replaces me, and I'd be 63. I'd still have wages for four years, which is a lot more than most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get on every course going and volunteer to be the operator who works alongside the robot cell. I'd ask the firm for an honest plan in writing. And I'd move some of the savings into something steady, because I'll need it to bridge the years between work and the pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'm not panicking, but it would be hard to sleep the first week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Jonas, my partner, and run the numbers on stopping at 61. Then I'd work out what I'd like to do instead, which is probably teach tech to older people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can the firm cope in two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is not enough for the firm to retrain 80 people. It would be a rush and some of them wouldn't get a chance.

fieldNote: She welcomes thinking AI but names the **robot** date as her real risk.

steps.text: Take every AI and robot-operation course the firm offers

Move part of the savings into a steady bond fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years feels like the sweet spot. I'd tell people it's enough time if you start. I'd run a few lunchtime sessions at the dairy and show how the AI reads a stop log.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd be fine in this one. Robots come in 2034, I'd be 66, and I'd already be retired. I'd think about the younger ones, though. Somebody like Tomas, 32, with two small kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools every day and push the firm to put two or three operators on a proper course, with me as the trainer. I'd also use the time to paint the house and do the things I keep saying I will. I'd carry on saving until 62.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It gives me time, and time is what I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your granddaughter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's 19 and studying design. I'd say learn to make things with your hands as well as a screen, and stay close to whichever tool does the boring part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the firm that retraining half the line later costs more than starting this year. It's a simple sum.

S3.quote: I'd tell the firm that retraining half the line later costs more than starting this year.
fieldNote: She turns spare time into **teaching**, which suits her adaptive streak.
Her calm rests on being retired before the robots arrive.
Takes a practical, cost-based case to management.

steps.text: Offer to train two or three operators on the AI log tool

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years I'd call a gift. I'd say to anyone who'll listen, use it as a gift, and learn something new every year. It won't wait for you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be retired by 62 or 63 and enjoying it. It's not my job that's at stake. I think about my granddaughter and whether she'll find steady work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and learning for four more years, then retire and volunteer teaching older people to use these tools. I'd keep my savings steady, and help my granddaughter with her course fees. I might even go back to the college for a short course on robotics, just to see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Curious. A bit sentimental about the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you hope the dairy looks like then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hope there are still people on the floor, working alongside the machines. If a robot runs the filler, I hope the first person it asks for help is a person like Tomas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, yes, I'd miss the line. The sound of the filler at six in the morning is the best alarm clock I've had.

say: Ten years is a **gift**; learn something new every year, because it won't wait for you.
I'd tell anyone who'll listen to treat the time as a **gift**.
think: I'd be retired by 62 or 63 and enjoying it, so it's my **granddaughter's** future I think about.
do: Work and keep learning for **four years**, then retire.
Volunteer to teach older people to use AI tools.
Help my granddaughter with her **course fees**.
feel: **Calm** and curious, and a bit sentimental about the line.
S4.quote: I hope there are still people on the floor, working alongside the machines.
fieldNote: Her longer view is **generous**: she sees time as a chance to teach.
Sentimental about the work, which softens her adaptability.
Money for her granddaughter is a quiet priority.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Not for me so much as for the people on the line who aren't used to this stuff. What would help is honest training from the firm and a government that pays people to retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people think I'm fearless with technology, and I'm not. I just try things in small bites. If more firms let their operators play with it, we'd all be calmer.

headlineQuote: People think I'm fearless with technology, and I'm not. I just try things in small bites.
portrait: Hana (**58**, lead operator on a milk bottling line) is curious and uses AI **every day** on her stop logs.
She feels secure: strong savings, a good pension and retirement around 62 mean the thinking AI feels like a tool.
Her real risk is the **robot** date in 2031, which she names herself and plans for.
She worries about colleagues like Birgit and Tomas, and turns spare time into teaching others.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario worries her most, because the firm can't retrain 80 people in two years.
whatWouldHelp: Honest **training** from the firm and government pay for retraining.
